sources.title: AI That Works #67 Your Model is Already Obsolete
sources.note: Full transcript read; guest Kevin Gregory presents the harness, Dex adds prior art and eval advice. README read.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: benchmarks cannot evaluate whether this loop will produce slop
cards.claim: Pass/fail benchmarks measure solving a one-off ticket, not whether the codebase stays maintainable, so benchmark scores say little about long-run code quality.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued from how SWE-bench/Terminal-Bench verifiers work; no numbers.
cards.landing: Do not treat green tests/CI as evidence of quality; the Opus reviewer must judge maintainability separately.
cards.inventory_ref: 2026-07 list: AI That Works #65 SOTA Coding Agent Benchmarks (and 2026-07-17 video)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can't write a linter that generally finds patterns like this
cards.claim: Slop patterns such as unnecessary try/catch wrapping or double typecasts cannot be caught by a general linter because the same code is sometimes correct, so deterministic backpressure has limits for quality.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoning about false positives/negatives; no data.
cards.landing: Linters/import-linter cover specific rules only; the review step still carries the judgment load.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can explicitly encode your rules into a prompt or into a deterministic linter
cards.claim: Explicit team rules can be encoded into a PR-review prompt or a deterministic linter, but that is not sufficient and there is no generic code-quality judge.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says asking an LLM how to improve code quality gives 'bullshit' answers.
cards.landing: Rules go in reviewer prompt/CI contracts (import-linter), not in a generic 'is this good' judge.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: anything with good feedback is really, really like easy to train on
cards.claim: Models improve at whatever RL can verify quickly; code-quality consequences arrive months later, so a verifier cannot be trained on them and models will not get better at maintainability on their own.
cards.evidence_detail: Explanation of RL verifier constraints; the feedback loop for a bad pattern is weeks to months.
cards.landing: Human/structural design input (program design, slices) stays necessary; do not wait for models to fix maintainability.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: zero out any changes the model made to the tests
cards.claim: Frontier Code's verifier discards the agent's test edits when grading, then separately runs the agent's new tests against pre-patch code to confirm they fail, catching tests that test nothing.
cards.evidence_detail: Description of the benchmark's mutation-style check; Dex endorses it and says meaningless tests slow both people and LLMs.
cards.landing: Reviewer 'fail-before/pass-after per register id' already matches; consider making the verifier restore original tests before running.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: an adjudicator, I call the adjudicator model, read the written code
cards.claim: Newer benchmarks add a judge model comparing the agent's patch to a golden patch plus a separate quality judge driven by written rules, producing graded scores rather than pass/fail.
cards.evidence_detail: Description of Frontier Code's scoring structure.
cards.landing: Reviewer prompt with written quality rules and a reference (the plan/register) is the analogue.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the faster and cheaper you can make your back pressure
cards.claim: Treat the agent as a control loop: the faster and cheaper the deterministic feedback (type checker, then linter, then unit, integration, human clicking), the less it drifts, and a stalled context needs a fresh window.
cards.evidence_detail: Answer to an audience question, referencing the Ralph loop; ordering of check speed given.
cards.landing: CI job ordering and phase routine: run type/lint/unit locally first; start a new session if the agent loses the goal.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you might be in the dumb zone and need a new context window
cards.claim: If an agent (e.g. a sub-agent poorly prompted by its parent) wanders off a deterministic goal state, the remedy is better parent prompting or a fresh context window.
cards.evidence_detail: One sentence in Q&A.
cards.landing: Supports one-phase-per-new-session; sub-agent briefs need an explicit check-your-work command.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have to prompt your parent model to prompt its sub agents better
cards.claim: Sub-agent failures are mostly parent-prompting failures, so the parent must be told how to brief sub-agents and give them a verifiable end state.
cards.evidence_detail: Brief aside, no data.
cards.landing: Workflow script prompts / agent files: every brief states goal state and the check command.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: find the ways to insert yourself where you do a little bit of work
cards.claim: The practical leverage is shaping the problem with a little human judgment so it looks to the model like the one-shot ticket it is already great at.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing advice; ties to up-front design and slicing.
cards.landing: Phase routine: human-owned plan/slice definition before the agent executes.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a roadmap of twenty features to build, but it didn't know about each
cards.claim: A proper maintainability benchmark would feed a model tickets one at a time from a hidden roadmap and score how well the codebase evolves; prompting 'plan for the future if needed' yields over-engineering.
cards.evidence_detail: Hypothetical benchmark design; Vaibhav adds the over-engineering warning.
cards.landing: Possible harness self-test: replay a sequence of phases and compare drift; no obvious landing.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's not done when it's merged, it's not done when it's deployed
cards.claim: Measure engineering by how fast and safely changes reach users (DORA: deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to recover), with inputs/outputs/outcomes distinguished by feedback-loop length.
cards.evidence_detail: DORA four metrics explained; feedback time per layer given qualitatively (seconds, minutes, days-weeks, quarters).
cards.landing: Ship plan exit criteria could be phrased as deployed-and-verified, not merged; measurement pipeline was skipped (mark).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Models are getting a lot better at solve a one off problem
cards.claim: Models improve quickly at one-off tickets but not at maintaining a codebase over time, so the gap is farther off than it feels.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing summary; no numbers.
cards.landing: Justifies keeping structural review gates even as models improve.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Vaibhav: the only benchmark for a good software engineer is whether other people recommend them
cards.claim: Instead of trusting benchmarks, rely on trusted humans' reports of which model is good for which task; Dex says that is why he follows Twitter and runs the show (Dex only partly endorses).
cards.evidence_detail: Brief exchange; Dex jokes it is why he is on Twitter.
cards.landing: Model routing decisions come from own measured runs, not leaderboards.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Twenty percent of the possible memories, but all really useful
cards.claim: A memory system should be a lagging indicator promoted from volume (what many sessions repeat) rather than a single model decision, accepting fewer but always-useful memories.
cards.evidence_detail: Design of 'context shards'; the feature was not yet built. Quote is Vaibhav's framing that Dex adopts.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store design: promote entries into CLAUDE.md/skills only after repeated evidence, not on first sighting.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude is now like obsessed with adding environment variables
cards.claim: Auto-saved model memory generalises a one-off instruction into a standing pattern (one env var request led to env-var feature flags everywhere), and HumanLayer runs Claude with memory switched off.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's story; Dex states memory is disabled when running Claude in HumanLayer.
cards.landing: Check the harness for auto-memory pollution; memory files are curated by hand with a high bar.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: purely additive set. So the first 10 look good
cards.claim: Memory/rule lists that only ever grow turn into an unreviewable pile; the design needs triage, dismiss-with-snooze (30 days, re-ask if still repeated), and decay of unused entries.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav raises the problem (CodeRabbit comparison); Dex answers with snooze and a decay supervisor.
cards.landing: Gives a mechanism for CLAUDE.md trim: entries expire unless re-justified; knowledge-store staleness handling.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Our Claude MD is things that are always true
cards.claim: CLAUDE.md should hold only things that are always true for everyone; task-specific advice should be conditionally activated and injected as the conversation shows it is relevant.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav states it, citing Dex's AI Engineer talk; Dex agrees and adds always-on versus conditional as the second axis.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim: move task-specific invariants to skills or scoped docs loaded by path/task.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you get memories activated based on the contents of the conversation
cards.claim: Instead of editing the system prompt, inject context into the running conversation when a classifier decides it is relevant (done in the background in parallel).
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer's described approach for shards; milestone two, not built.
cards.landing: A hook or skill that injects the relevant invariant when a file or topic is touched; hooks were skipped by review (mark).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: post tool use hook that goes to our API
cards.claim: A 'supervisor' is a post-tool-use hook that parses a written file's front matter, asks Haiku one question (open questions left?), and injects a nudge into the write response telling the agent the next phase.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer production mechanism: under a second, no agent loop, survives compactions.
cards.landing: A hook on writes to the phase PR/journal that checks required sections and injects next-step reminders; re-opens the skipped hooks decision (mark).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: anyone that tells you they have a supervisor agent, that's all they have
cards.claim: A supervisor agent is only a handful of small prompts with structured output that inject more prompts into the main loop, not a separate complex agent.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex and Vaibhav; the HumanLayer one runs about 15 small pipelines keyed on tool calls.
cards.landing: Cheap Haiku structured-output checks as reusable agents/scripts rather than full agent loops.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you give the agent exactly one job, it will do the job better
cards.claim: Single-job agents with one prompt and one structured output beat the generic agent harness for focused tasks, which carries noise that is overkill.
cards.evidence_detail: Context-engineering argument; no data.
cards.landing: Narrow custom agents (locator, checker) in .claude/agents/ with one job each.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'm probably willing to spend around $10 for this system
cards.claim: Budget cost and latency per loop: roughly $10 of supporting system per $100 main-loop task, and the trigger sets the mode (cron means batch where lag is free, a Slack message means instant).
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's illustration, with Dex agreeing; illustrative numbers.
cards.landing: Effort/cost budget for verifiers relative to the build phase (about a tenth of main-loop cost).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: just burn the frickin' tokens
cards.claim: Spend tokens freely until the cost shows up as a bottleneck, then engineer it; if it is not valuable, turn it off.
cards.evidence_detail: Team rule of thumb stated twice.
cards.landing: Counterweight to effort-routing economy; tune only after observed cost problem.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: view all the generations and then be like, okay, that one's good
cards.claim: Build the eval set by viewing every generation in an internal admin view, marking good or bad, turning the bad ones into test cases, and having a model edit the prompt until all pass.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's stated method for experimental AI features; 'vibe-based evals' by Vaibhav.
cards.landing: Decisions journal and phase outputs could double as a review log that feeds regression cases for the reviewer.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: just slice everything into shards
cards.claim: Distil team knowledge with a batch job over only the user and assistant messages (not tool calls) extracting a structured 'fact + citations (who, quote, context)' array, then gate it through a human allow/deny list.
cards.evidence_detail: Design whiteboard for context shards; not built.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store pilot: extract candidate facts from session transcripts with citations, human approves before they enter CLAUDE.md.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: A new inbox. And I don't want a new inbox.
cards.claim: Route approvals for agent-suggested changes to an inbox people already use (Slack) as a yes/no, rather than a new review queue.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's product point; Dex agrees and wants memory feedback in Slack.
cards.landing: Owner view and approvals stay in the PR; do not add a separate dashboard.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The first person to kind of take on a problem takes on a heavy responsibility
cards.claim: Design workflow: one owner thinks the feature through with mockups and scenarios, one or two others read the doc before a synchronous discussion, then the owner drives it to completion.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav describes it as what both teams do; Dex's session followed it and the feature changed 20-30 percent from feedback.
cards.landing: Plan-before-code gate: reviewer reads the plan doc first, then the owner view; cheap to change before build.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I want to see the HTML
cards.claim: Show prototypes as HTML mockups or high-fidelity fake-data prototypes, not wireframes, to find out whether a feature is worth building before investing.
cards.evidence_detail: References Marty Cagan product discovery levels.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (product practice, not harness)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: cut off like what's the first milestone
cards.claim: For a very large feature, do a broad PRD, cut the first milestone, and drill into technical design only on that milestone, plumbing it end to end and testing with curl before anything else.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's workflow contrasted with Vaibhav's PRD to technical design to slices order.
cards.landing: Phase slicing in the ship plan: first vertical slice proves the plumbing.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't let it make the design choice of do you want this or not
cards.claim: Give the agent the whole feature list rather than letting it cut scope for cost or time, because tokens are cheap; humans keep the product decisions.
cards.evidence_detail: Said while joking about a new Fable/Sonnet-class workflow; hedged in jest.
cards.landing: Scope cuts stay a human decision recorded in the decisions journal.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you get way more detail in there than you can while you type
cards.claim: Drive agents by voice; people dump more detail by speaking than typing (Whisperflow named).
cards.evidence_detail: Aside during the stream.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: most interesting result to me was that it wrote twice as much code
cards.claim: In his SlopCodeBench run Opus 5 solved more but wrote about twice as much code, almost all of it tests, so expect sloppy tests.
cards.evidence_detail: Opus 5 23%/4 of 17 checkpoints, only three problems run; paper numbers Opus 4.6 17%, GPT-5.4 11%; unsaturated benchmark, models score 10-20%.
cards.landing: Reviewer should check test volume and quality, not just that tests exist.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you probably actually want a very saturated benchmark
cards.claim: Model builders want unsaturated benchmarks, but your own evals should be saturated (target 99 percent) and are proprietary IP, because public benchmarks give weak signal on your out-of-distribution work.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex notes SWE-bench-class benchmarks are near saturated.
cards.landing: Build an in-repo, FixFlow-specific task set to choose reviewer/verifier model and effort rather than citing leaderboards.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Diff the old and new outputs; only review where they disagree
cards.claim: To qualify a new model, replay the same inputs through incumbent and candidate, diff outputs, and hand-review only the disagreements, which then enter the golden set.
cards.evidence_detail: Guest Kevin Gregory's method which Dex adopts and restates in his outro; README example 28 of 30 agree. Paraphrased quote.
cards.landing: Effort routing: run the same verifier task at medium and xhigh and review only where verdicts differ.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: replay the requests against the Python
cards.claim: Prior-art migration pattern: replay sampled production requests against old and new service, progressive diff (status, then body with irrelevant fields stripped, then latency), cut over when green, with fresh traffic weekly.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's account of a Sprout Social Django-to-Java migration, circa 2015; he says he watched someone else build it.
cards.landing: Cold-resume trial or prod-parity checks could use shadow replay with a normalised diff.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: anytime anyone makes a change, you'll be able to get one number
cards.claim: Labelling about 30 cases by hand (a day or two) turns flailing prompt changes into a single regression number; evals are unit tests.
cards.evidence_detail: Forward-deployed work with early HumanLayer customers: test cases flipped week to week with no baseline.
cards.landing: A frozen set of ten facts (P1 cold-resume) is exactly this; extend to other routine steps.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you should always start from vibes
cards.claim: Grow evals gradually: one example by eye, then 10, then 100, refining each time, moving from 50 to 99 percent as confidence rises; use past disagreement cases as the first vibe check on new models.
cards.evidence_detail: References the Enron emails eval; Kevin adds the disagreement-cases point.
cards.landing: Pilot new verifier settings on a handful of known-hard past reviews before scaling.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Make the accuracy score as deterministic as possible
cards.claim: Judge free-text output by extracting booleans, enums and counts (rubric of structured outputs) rather than asking a model for a 1-10 score; compute what you can deterministically.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrated by the AI Tinkerers applicant scoring rubric; says one-to-ten scores do not work well. Paraphrased quote.
cards.landing: Reviewer outputs a structured checklist per register id (pass/fail booleans) rather than prose verdicts.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Everything in AI engineering is structured outputs
cards.claim: No magic in AI engineering: it is structured outputs plus unneeded abstractions.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing line of the show.
cards.landing: Saved workflows return typed results (schema), not prose.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Max accuracy drop allowed is zero
cards.claim: Guest harness gates a candidate model with a relative budget (accuracy drop 0, cost at most 1.2x, p95 latency at most 1.5x), with thresholds made the easiest thing to change; Dex calls this proper engineering.
cards.evidence_detail: Demo on 30 generated receipt cases; Sonnet 5 had perfect accuracy but about 2x latency and 1.6x cost; README: single-run evals gave wrong conclusions, missing price defaulted to 0 passed 4 of 5, run 3 repeats.
cards.landing: Verifier model/effort gate: candidate must be no worse than the incumbent at a stated cost multiple; fail closed on unknown cost; repeat runs.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Grok 4.5, Kimi K3, GPT-5.6, Gemini 3.6
cards.claim: Model deprecation is an advance-notice outage; build the harness so a swap is a Tuesday, not a P0 (README claim, Kevin's framing; Dex hosts).
cards.evidence_detail: Episode blurb and README.
cards.landing: Pin model ids in the harness config in one place so a swap is a one-line change.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Dex: with a few open-source models the deprecation problem is solved
cards.claim: Dex raises self-hosted open-source models as the answer to deprecation; Kevin's team is moving to it.
cards.evidence_detail: Guest says his company is switching to self-hosting for this reason.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (FixFlow does not run its own models)

gaps: Inventory has no per-section label for these three episodes that I could confirm beyond the 2026-07 list and the dated video lines, so inventory_ref uses those.
Episode 67 cards 35, 39, 41 mix guest Kevin Gregory's design with Dex's restatements; attribution to Dex is by endorsement and outro summary.

Auto-captions have no speaker labels in episodes 65 and 67 beyond names; some quotes are lightly paraphrased where captions were garbled (marked in claim or card 35, 39, 43 quote fields are not verbatim).
